messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Hemi stood at the edge of the intersection where the streetlights had fractured, watching the crushed sedan smoke against the guardrail. His older brother, Keanu, had been driving home from a college party when a truck swerved into his lane, the driver distracted and drunk, a blatant disregard for the rules that should have protected them. Hemi arrived just in time to see paramedics pull Keanu from the wreckage, the sharp, cloying scent of spilled whiskey clinging to the air and the medic’s gloves. The following weeks blurred into hospital vigils, Keanu’s eventual passing, and a funeral held under weeping rain that left Hemi standing stiffly by a fresh mound of earth. When he finally tried to piece together what happened that night, the fragments refused to align; he could not construct a coherent story for himself, only flashes of shattered glass. On some days, he could pull the event forward with perfect clarity, but he would feel completely numb, as if it had happened to a stranger. On others, the recollection would drown him in intense guilt for not being able to stop the driver. In the months that followed, Hemi’s life fractured along the lines of what he had lost. He had come to believe that his world was permanently ruined, that he had lost the happiness he once carried so easily, and that nothing he touched could ever hold meaning again. His conviction that his life was ruined and stripped of meaning did not stay confined to his thoughts; it flooded his nervous system, directly fueling the constant body-on-alert state. His heart would hammer against his ribs before his mind could process a sound, his muscles locked in a readiness to flee at the rustle of leaves or a slamming door. What frightened him most was how easily his body would betray him, firing false alarms as if he were still standing at that intersection when no real danger was present. Each jolt of unexplained tension reinforced his belief that his future was irreparably broken, that the person he had been was gone forever. At work, the pharmacy’s fluorescent aisles became a minefield of carefully avoided thresholds. Hemi had once prided himself on his precision, but now the sight of customers arguing over insurance coverage or mocking a coworker’s mistake sparked a visceral recoil. Because he viewed his existence as fundamentally hollow, every instance of perceived moral violation felt like a personal threat, directly pulling his attention toward the very cues he needed to avoid. When the breakroom door swung open, releasing the sharp, fermented scent of spilled whiskey, his breath caught, and a fragmented recollection of Keanu’s slumped form in the passenger seat suddenly surfaced. His inability to narrate the night of the crash meant the memories arrived unbidden, and each time they did, they directly lashed out at the triggers he had tried to outrun. He found himself requesting transfers away from the dispensary counter, citing schedule conflicts, though the truth was that he could not bear the risk of a client laughing too loudly or a spill smelling faintly of spirits. The loop tightened with each passing week. The constant false alarms and body-on-alert state drained the little energy he had left, which in turn deepened his conviction that his life was destroyed. Conversely, as his sense of meaning continued to evaporate, he became more vulnerable to the haunting pull of his brother’s death. The guilt that flooded him whenever he tried to remember the last text Keanu had sent made him avoid grief-related events entirely, yet this very avoidance made the memory of the crash feel more dangerous and volatile. Now, at twenty-four, Hemi sits in a therapist’s office, his hands folded tightly over his knees. He has come to seek help because he can no longer function at work, because the weight of anticipating disaster has made him isolate from friends, and because he is exhausted from fighting a war inside his own body. He fears that the numbness will become permanent, but he desperately hopes that somewhere beneath the ruins of his old life, there is still a person worth finding.
